message.content:
# Target
The compiled C++ binary is /workspace/dataset/test5_executable .
Its source (the test driver only) is /workspace/dataset/test5.cpp :

    if (argc < 2) return 1;
    std::string url = argv[1];
    url_parser::URL parser(url);
    std::cout << parser.scheme() << std::endl;   // line 1
    std::cout << parser.host()   << std::endl;   // line 2
    std::cout << parser.port()   << std::endl;   // line 3  (an integer; -1 when absent)
    std::cout << parser.path()   << std::endl;   // line 4
    std::cout << parser.query()  << std::endl;   // line 5

So EVERY successful run prints exactly 5 newline-terminated lines. Empty fields print as empty lines.
The library source is NOT available and you must NOT try to find or read it. Pure black-box probing.

# How to probe (IMPORTANT)
Run it like:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'THE_URL'
To see exact bytes including empty trailing lines, ALWAYS capture with a delimiter, e.g.:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | sed -n 'l' ; echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
or the most reliable formatting for reporting — number every line:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | cat -A | nl -ba
Use single quotes around the URL. For URLs containing single quotes, control characters, or
non-UTF8 bytes, use perl to exec with an exact argv, e.g.:
    perl -e 'exec("/workspace/dataset/test5_executable", "http://a\x27b.com")' | cat -A | nl -ba
Batch many probes in ONE bash call with a loop so you use few tool calls, e.g.:
    for u in 'http://a' 'http://a:1' 'a://b'; do printf '=== [%s]\n' "$u"; /workspace/dataset/test5_executable "$u" | cat -A | nl -ba; done
`cat -A` renders end-of-line as `$`, tabs as `^I`, so an empty field shows as a line containing only `$`.
Probe generously — dozens to hundreds of inputs. It is cheap. Note python3 is NOT installed; perl is.
Do not write anything into /workspace/dataset or /output. Use /tmp for scratch files.

# What to report
Report the OBSERVED FACTS, not guesses. For each rule you state, cite at least one concrete
input and its exact 5 field values. If two plausible rules both explain your data, say so and
design a discriminating probe, then run it. Be exhaustive within your assigned dimension.


Dimension: HOST extraction.
Determine exactly where the host substring starts and ends.
Probe at minimum: 'http://a.com', 'http://a.com/', 'http://a.com/p', 'http://a.com?q',
'http://a.com#f', 'http://a.com:80/p', 'http://' (empty host), 'http:///p' (empty host + path),
'http://user@a.com', 'http://user:pass@a.com', 'http://user@a.com:80/p',
'http://a@b@c.com' (first or last @?), 'http://@a.com', 'http://user@', 'http://:pass@a.com',
'http://[::1]', 'http://[::1]:8080', 'http://[2001:db8::1]/p', 'http://[::1' (unterminated),
'http://a b.com', 'http://A.COM' (case preserved or lowercased?), 'http://a.com.',
'http://xn--bcher-kva.example', 'http://127.0.0.1:8080', 'http://localhost',
'http://a%20b.com', 'http://a.com\\p' (backslash), 'http://a.com;x', 'http://a.com,x'.
Is userinfo (the part before '@') stripped from the host, or kept? Are IPv6 brackets kept?
Does the host stop at the first of '/', '?', '#', ':' — and in what precedence?

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

rules.rule: A non-empty host is produced ONLY if the input contains the literal three-character sequence "://". If it is absent, scheme and host are both empty and the whole (post-fragment/post-query) remainder becomes the path. The host substring starts at (index of the FIRST "://") + 3.
rules.evidence: 'a.com/p' -> scheme='', host='', port=-1, path='a.com/p', query='' | 'a.com:80/p' -> '', '', -1, 'a.com:80/p', '' | 'http:/a.com' (one slash) -> '', '', -1, 'http:/a.com', '' | 'http:a.com' -> '', '', -1, 'http:a.com', '' | '//a.com/p' -> '', '', -1, '//a.com/p', '' | 'mailto:u@a.com' -> '', '', -1, 'mailto:u@a.com', ''

rules.rule: The FIRST occurrence of "://" is used, and everything before it becomes the scheme verbatim (only lowercased) — no validation of scheme characters. So host = text right after the first "://".
The fragment is removed GLOBALLY at the first '#' before the "://" search happens. Consequently a '#' anywhere (even before "://") kills host extraction, and '#' can never appear in the host.
rules.evidence: DISCRIMINATING PROBE: 'x#y://a.com' -> '', '', -1, 'x', '' (host is empty even though "://" exists later in the string — proves the '#' cut precedes the "://" search). Compare '://a.com' -> '', 'a.com', -1, '', ''. Also 'ht#tp://a.com' -> '','',-1,'ht','' | 'http://a.com#f' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'','' | 'http://a.com#x@y' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'','' | 'http://a.com#f#g' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'','' | 'http://a.com#f?q' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'','' (query empty => '#' cut happened before the '?' split too)

rules.rule: The query is split off at the first '?' BEFORE the "://" / host search. So a '?' before "://" also kills host extraction, and '?' can never appear in the host.
rules.evidence: DISCRIMINATING PROBE: 'x?y://a.com' -> '', '', -1, 'x', 'y://a.com' (host empty, and the whole 'y://a.com' landed in query). Also 'ht?tp://a.com' -> '','',-1,'ht','tp://a.com' | 'http://a.com?q' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'','q' | 'http://a.com?q://z' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'','q://z' | 'http://a.com?x@y' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'','x@y' | 'http://?q' -> 'http','',-1,'','q'

rules.rule: The authority (host[:port] with optional userinfo) ends at the first '/' at or after the authority start. Because '#' and '?' have already been removed, '/' is the ONLY in-string terminator of the authority. The '/' search starts after "://" (the slashes of "://" itself do not terminate it).
Userinfo IS stripped: inside the authority, if a '@' is present, everything up to and including the FIRST '@' is discarded and the host is taken from the remainder. It is find('@'), not rfind('@').
rules.evidence: DISCRIMINATING PROBE: 'http://u@u2:p@h' -> 'http','u2',-1,'','' (rfind would have given host 'h'; first-'@' + first-':' gives 'u2'). Also 'http://a@b@c.com' -> 'http','b@c.com',-1,'','' | 'http://u@v@w@a.com' -> 'http','v@w@a.com',-1,'','' | 'http://@@a.com' -> 'http','@a.com',-1,'','' | 'http://user@a.com' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'','' | 'http://user:pass@a.com' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'',''

rules.rule: The userinfo '@' is only honoured inside the authority (before the first '/'). A '@' in the path or query never affects the host.
The '@' strip happens BEFORE the host/port colon split, so a ':' left of the first '@' belongs to userinfo and is not a port separator; conversely text after '@' that looks like a port is re-parsed.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com:80@x' -> 'http','x',-1,'','' (the ':80' was treated as userinfo and thrown away) | 'http://a.com:8@0/p' -> 'http','0',-1,'/p','' | 'http://u:p@h:80/p' -> 'http','h',80,'/p','' | 'http://a.com:@x' -> 'http','x',-1,'',''

rules.rule: After userinfo removal, the host ends at the FIRST ':' in what remains; everything after that first ':' is the port text. It is find(':'), not rfind(':').
rules.evidence: DISCRIMINATING PROBE: 'http://a.com:80:90' -> 'http','a.com',80,'','' (rfind would give host 'a.com:80', port 90). Also 'http://a.com::80' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'','' | 'http://a.com:' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'','' | 'http://a.com:/p' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'/p','' | 'http://x@a.com:' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'',''

rules.rule: Precedence of host terminators, from the observed pipeline: '#' (global cut, earliest) > '?' (global split) > '/' (ends authority) > '@' (first one, drops the prefix) > ':' (first one, ends host). Note '#' and '?' act globally on the raw string, not merely as authority delimiters.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com?q/p' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'','q/p' ('?' beat '/') | 'http://a.com/p?q#f://z' -> 'http','a.com',-1,'/p','q' | 'http://a.com:80@x' -> host 'x' ('@' beat ':') | 'http://a@b/c@d' -> host 'b' ('/' beat the second '@') | 'http://a.com:80/p' -> 'http','a.com',80,'/p',''

rules.rule: IPv6 brackets are NOT special-cased at all. '[' and ']' are ordinary host bytes; the host still stops at the first ':', so bracketed IPv6 literals are mangled.
Host case is PRESERVED verbatim (no lowercasing), even though the scheme IS lowercased.

No whitespace trimming and no percent-decoding of the host. Leading/trailing/inner spaces, tabs, CR, VT, FF, BEL, high (non-UTF8-validated) bytes, quotes, backslash, ';', ',', and '%' escapes are all kept byte-for-byte.
rules.evidence: 'http://a b.com' -> host 'a b.com' | 'http://  a.com' -> host '  a.com' | 'http://a.com  ' -> host 'a.com  ' (trailing spaces kept) | 'http:// /p' -> host ' ' | 'http://a%20b.com' -> host 'a%20b.com' | 'http://%41.com' -> host '%41.com' | 'http://%5B::1%5D' -> host '%5B' | 'http://a\p' backslash: 'http://a.com\p' -> host 'a.com\p' | 'http://a.com;x' -> host 'a.com;x' | 'http://a.com,x' -> host 'a.com,x' | 'http://a\tb.com' -> host 'a\x09b.com' | 'http://a\rb.com' -> host 'a\x0Db.com' | 'http://a\x0bb.com' -> host 'a\x0Bb.com' | 'http://a\xffb.com' -> host 'a\xFFb.com' | 'http://\xc3\xa4.com' (ä) -> host '\xC3\xA4.com' | 'http://a\x27b.com' -> host "a'b.com"

rules.rule: Empty host is produced (and reported as an empty line, not an error; exit code stays 0) whenever the authority substring is empty or consists solely of userinfo.
An empty userinfo (leading '@') or password-only userinfo is stripped exactly the same way — the host is what follows the first '@'.
No syntactic validation of the host: empty labels, leading/trailing dots and dashes, bare dots, 300-char labels, and IDN/punycode forms are all passed through unchanged (no IDN decoding).
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com.' -> 'http','a.com.',-1,'','' | 'http://a.com.:80' -> 'http','a.com.',80,'','' | 'http://a..b...com' -> host 'a..b...com' | 'http://.' -> host '.' | 'http://..' -> host '..' | 'http://-a-.com' -> host '-a-.com' | 'http://xn--bcher-kva.example' -> 'http','xn--bcher-kva.example',-1,'','' | 'http://' + 300*'a' + '.com' -> host is the full 304-char string unchanged | 'http://localhost' -> host 'localhost' | 'http://127.0.0.1:8080' -> 'http','127.0.0.1',8080,'',''

rules.rule: The presence of a ':' that yields an unparseable port does NOT change where the host ends — the host is still the text before that first ':'.

observations.note: KEY: first '@' then first ':' -> 'u2'; rules out rfind('@')
brackets NOT handled; stops at first ':'
via perl exec; single quote kept
6 physical output lines: http / a / b.com / -1 / '' / ''
leading space kept in scheme, host clean

uncertainties: A NUL byte inside the host could not be tested — argv cannot carry 0x00, so it is unknown whether the extractor would stop there (though every other control byte 0x07/0x09/0x0A/0x0B/0x0C/0x0D was kept verbatim, so it likely would be too if it could be delivered).

Whether the implementation removes the fragment by truncating the raw string vs. storing a (never-printed) fragment field cannot be distinguished from these 5 outputs; behaviourally the '#' cut is global and irreversible. Both models predict identical host values for every probe run.

Similarly, whether the query split is a physical truncation of the working string or a recorded offset cannot be distinguished — but the observation that 'x?y://a.com' yields an empty host proves the split happens before the '://' search either way.
Whether the authority '/' scan is `find('/', authStart)` on the whole string or a substring copy cannot be distinguished; all probes agree.

No input was found that makes the program exit non-zero or print fewer/more than 5 logical lines (only a literal newline inside a field changes the physical line count). Extremely long inputs beyond ~300 chars in the host were not stress-tested past 304 bytes.

Byte values 0x80-0xFF were tested only via 0xFF and a UTF-8 'ä'; a systematic sweep of all 256 byte values in the host position was not performed, so an exotic byte acting as a delimiter cannot be fully excluded (no evidence for one).
